title: Human Pancreas Anatomy: Ducts, Exocrine Acini & Hormone
description: Understand human pancreas anatomy, from the head, neck, body, and tail to the main pancreatic duct, digestive enzyme acini, and endocrine islet cell types.
h1: Human Pancreas Anatomy: Regions, Ducts, Acini and Endocrine Islets
blurb: A dual-function retroperitoneal gland: exocrine acini secrete bicarbonate and digestive enzymes into the duodenum while endocrine islets regulate blood glucose.
lead: Curled into the C-shaped loop of the duodenum behind the stomach, the pancreas works a double shift as both an enzyme factory for digestion and a hormone regulator. In this illustrated guide to human pancreas anatomy, we examine 21 documented structures—including head, neck, body, tail—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Curled into the C-shaped loop of the duodenum behind the stomach, the pancreas works a double shift as both an enzyme factory for digestion and a hormone regulator. The pancreas is both an exocrine and an endocrine organ. Acinar cells package trypsinogen, lipase and amylase into zymogen granules and secrete them into the pancreatic duct, which joins the common bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla; bicarbonate-rich fluid from duct cells neutralises gastric acid. Scattered among the acini, the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin (beta cells), glucagon (alpha), somatostatin (delta) and pancreatic polypeptide directly into blood, minute-to-minute control of glucose. Within the human body, the pancreas (Pancreas) is situated in retroperitoneal, across L1–L2 behind the stomach, receives arterial perfusion via splenic artery + pancreaticoduodenal arcades, and is innervated by vagus + splanchnic via coeliac plexus.

The head (Caput pancreatis) is the broad end nestled in the C-loop of the duodenum, with the uncinate process hooking behind the superior mesenteric vessels. Physiologically, the head houses much of the exocrine tissue and the terminal duct. The neck (Collum pancreatis) is the short constriction in front of the portal vein's formation. Physiologically, the neck governs landmark separating head from body; the portal vein forms behind it. The body (Corpus pancreatis) is the middle third crossing the aorta and vertebral body, behind the stomach in the lesser sac. Physiologically, the body carries the duct and splenic vessels along its borders. The tail (Cauda pancreatis) is the narrow left end reaching the splenic hilum between the layers of the splenorenal ligament. Physiologically, the tail contains a high density of islets. The main pancreatic duct (Ductus pancreaticus) runs the length of the gland from tail to head, joining the common bile duct at the ampulla in the second part of duodenum. Physiologically, the main pancreatic duct delivers ~1.5 L of enzyme- and bicarbonate-rich juice daily. The accessory duct (of Santorini) (Ductus pancreaticus accessorius) is an inconstant second duct opening at the minor duodenal papilla above the main one. Physiologically, the accessory duct (of Santorini) provides alternative drainage, mainly of the head.

Clinically, regarding the head, a tumour here compresses the common bile duct, causing painless obstructive jaundice and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's law). From a diagnostic standpoint, in the neck, it is the transection line in a Whipple procedure and in distal pancreatectomy. In clinical pathology involving the body, it lies against the splenic vein — thrombosis of that vein from pancreatitis causes isolated gastric varices. Medical evaluation of the tail also notes that it is easily injured during splenectomy, causing a postoperative pancreatic fistula.

questions.question: What does the pancreas do?
questions.answer: Its exocrine tissue releases digestive enzymes into the small intestine. Endocrine islets release hormones such as insulin and glucagon into the blood. Structurally, the islets of Langerhans (Insulae pancreaticae) comprises 1–1.5 million microscopic clusters of alpha (glucagon), beta (insulin, amylin), delta (somatostatin) and PP cells, richly capillarised. Physiologically, the islets of Langerhans governs minute-to-minute control of blood glucose, plus intermediary metabolism.

questions.question: Where is the pancreas located?
questions.answer: It lies behind the stomach across the upper abdomen. Its head sits near the duodenum, while its tail reaches toward the spleen. The head (Caput pancreatis) is the broad end nestled in the C-loop of the duodenum, with the uncinate process hooking behind the superior mesenteric vessels. Physiologically, the head houses much of the exocrine tissue and the terminal duct.

questions.question: Where is the head of the pancreas?
questions.answer: The broad end nestled in the C-loop of the duodenum, with the uncinate process hooking behind the superior mesenteric vessels. Functionally, it houses much of the exocrine tissue and the terminal duct. Structurally, the uncinate process comprises hook-shaped pancreatic head extension passing posterior to superior mesenteric vessels. Physiologically, the uncinate process governs completes deep head contour around the mesenteric root.

questions.question: Where is the main pancreatic duct located?
questions.answer: Runs the length of the gland from tail to head, joining the common bile duct at the ampulla in the second part of duodenum. Functionally, it delivers ~1.5 L of enzyme- and bicarbonate-rich juice daily. Medical evaluation of the main pancreatic duct also notes that a "double duct sign" (dilated pancreatic and bile ducts) on imaging suggests a head tumour.

questions.question: What is the function of the acinar cells & ductules?
questions.answer: Functionally, it secrete the pro-enzymes for digesting protein, fat and carbohydrate. Grape-like clusters of enzyme-packed cells draining into centroacinar cells and ductules. Clinically, regarding the acinar cells & ductules, premature activation of trypsin inside acinar cells is the initiating event of acute pancreatitis.
